title: Misinformation in YouTube Videos About Chiropractic Treatment for Otitis Media.
screen_reason: Content analysis of a rank-truncated sample of 50 YouTube videos on chiropractic treatment for otitis media, with two claim-level misinformation themes reported as shares of the 50 videos (25 videos claiming manipulation can 'fix' the Eustachian tube; 14 videos, 28%, asserting nerve correction). Denominator = all videos in the sampled set, so the shares are CONTENT prevalence. Only the abstract was available, so no methods detail beyond it (no reliability statistic, no per-theme definitions).

estimates.country: United States (YouTube searched in US region)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 50 sampled chiropractic/otitis-media YouTube videos that claimed chiropractic manipulation could 'fix' the Eustachian tube (a coded misinformation theme)
estimates.denominator: 50 English-language YouTube videos, the first 50 ranked by relevance for three chiropractic/otitis-media search terms (Incognito mode, US region, January 2023)
estimates.definition: Video coded by two independent reviewers as containing the misinformation theme that chiropractic manipulation can 'fix' the Eustachian tube; a third reviewer resolved discrepancies
estimates.misinfo_def: coded for references to evidence-based therapies, chiropractic techniques, and misinformation themes ('fixing' nerves or the Eustachian tube)
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-five videos claimed that chiropractic manipulation could "fix" the Eustachian tube, and 14 videos (28%) asserted nerve correction; none mentioned antibiotics or tympanostomy tubes.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers coded misinformation themes; a third reviewer resolved discrepancies. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported in the abstract. Promoted techniques were cross-checked against a parallel PubMed search, which found 'limited or low-quality supporting evidence'.
estimates.moderator_quote: YouTube was searched in January 2023 (Incognito mode, US region) using the terms "chiropractic treatment for otitis media", "chiropractic ear infection", and "chiropractic ear problems". The first 50 English-language videos ranked by relevance were evaluated.
estimates.notes: Share computed as an exact part/whole from the verbatim count 25 over the verbatim denominator of 50 videos (R8-compliant). The abstract reports no overall '% of videos containing any misinformation', so this row is one of two claim-type shares and must NOT be summed with the nerve-correction row (the two themes may overlap in the same video). breadth coded 'misleading' rather than 'false' because the abstract frames the claims as unverified/unsupported ('unverified claims', 'limited or low-quality supporting evidence') rather than fact-checked false. country coded United States because only the search region is stated as US; the videos themselves are not restricted to US creators.

estimates.country: United States (YouTube searched in US region)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 50 sampled chiropractic/otitis-media YouTube videos that asserted nerve correction (a coded misinformation theme)
estimates.denominator: 50 English-language YouTube videos, the first 50 ranked by relevance for three chiropractic/otitis-media search terms (Incognito mode, US region, January 2023)
estimates.definition: Video coded by two independent reviewers as asserting nerve correction by chiropractic manipulation (a coded misinformation theme); a third reviewer resolved discrepancies
estimates.misinfo_def: coded for references to evidence-based therapies, chiropractic techniques, and misinformation themes ('fixing' nerves or the Eustachian tube)
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-five videos claimed that chiropractic manipulation could "fix" the Eustachian tube, and 14 videos (28%) asserted nerve correction; none mentioned antibiotics or tympanostomy tubes.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers coded misinformation themes; a third reviewer resolved discrepancies. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: Two independent reviewers extracted metadata (views, duration, likes, comments, upload source) and coded for references to evidence-based therapies, chiropractic techniques, and misinformation themes ("fixing" nerves or the Eustachian tube); a third reviewer resolved discrepancies.
estimates.notes: Verbatim 28% with a verbatim numerator (14) and denominator (50 videos). Second of two claim-type shares; not additive with the Eustachian-tube row. Same abstract-only limitations as the other row.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 'Only three videos (6%) cited scientific sources' and 'none mentioned antibiotics or tympanostomy tubes' - both are absence/omission numerators (a share NOT doing something), not a share of items judged false or misleading; (b) 'Upper-cervical adjustments (32 videos, 64%) and ear-massage maneuvers (25 videos, 50%) were the most frequently promoted techniques' - these are shares of videos promoting a technique, and while the abstract notes the techniques have 'limited or low-quality supporting evidence', the paper's own misinformation coding is the two themes ('fixing' nerves or the Eustachian tube), so treating technique promotion as a misinformation share would over-read the abstract; (c) 'Chiropractors produced 42 videos (84% of the content)' and 'hospital or academic channels contributed two videos (4%)' - source-provenance shares, not falsity; (d) engagement totals (2,600,209 views, 21,102 likes, 1,766 comments) - no misinformation denominator attached, so no exposure/reach row is derivable. No overall misinformation prevalence share (% of videos containing any misinformation) is given anywhere in the abstract, despite the conclusion that misinformation 'is widespread'; an adjudicator wanting a single headline number should probably use the 50% Eustachian-tube theme, which is the largest single theme. Full text not available, so the definition of each theme, any reliability statistic, and whether the two themes overlap could not be checked.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis: three keyword searches in Incognito mode, US region, January 2023; first 50 English-language videos by relevance evaluated (rank-truncated, no random sampling); two independent reviewers extracted metadata and coded misinformation themes with a third reviewer resolving discrepancies; no inter-rater reliability statistic reported; descriptive statistics only; abstract-only text, so response/exclusion flow and codebook are unverifiable.
